concepts.gloss: A head word of a PP, classed here without requiring an NP complement or even any complement.
Selection by individual preposition heads among NP, PP, AdvP, clausal, and predicative AdjP complements.
A use of a preposition that expresses grammatical relations or assigned roles rather than an independently identifiable spatial or other meaning.
A use where the preposition contributes a recognisable independent meaning, as distinct from a grammaticised use.
A preposition that heads a PP without a complement; the same lexeme may optionally take a complement, or never take one.
An exceptional PP head that can follow its own complement, as with notwithstanding.
The relative position of a phrase head and its complement; the Cambridge preposition category is not defined by order alone.
A typological term that can cover both prepositions and postpositions without imposing a linear position on the category.
Traditional category of words introducing subordinate clauses; most of its members are classified as prepositions here, apart from the specified subordinators.

rules.concept: subordinators excluded from the preposition category
rules.statement: Cambridge treats traditional subordinating conjunctions as prepositions except whether, interrogative if equivalent to whether, and that when introducing a subordinate clause, which function as subordinators.
rules.condition: When classifying a word associated with a subordinate content clause, treat whether, if introducing an embedded interrogative, and clause-introducing that as subordination markers rather than heads; prepositions such as after may instead head PPs with clause complements.

contrast.text: The dancers rested after the music stopped. [after: preposition with declarative clause complement]
Mara wondered whether the music had stopped. [whether: subordinator]
Mara asked if the music had stopped. [interrogative if: subordinator]
Mara believed that the music had stopped. [that: subordinator]
If the music stops, the dancers will rest. [conditional if: preposition under Cambridge's analysis]

rules.review_notes: The three explicitly stated exceptions are lexical/use-specific; conditional if is not the interrogative-if exception. The original extraction AI and this approval action are not a separate second-pass review.

rules.statement: In grammaticised uses a preposition primarily signals a constructional or semantic role rather than a separately identifiable meaning, and these uses normally take NP complements and resist independent modification.
rules.condition: When by introduces the agent in a passive, of links an NP to a nominal head, or a selected preposition connects an NP to an adjective or verb, analyse the grammatical relation as a grammaticised use; distinguish spatial or other independently meaningful uses of the same preposition.

exceptions.description: A preposition that has grammaticised uses can also have non-grammaticised uses with an independently identifiable meaning; many prepositions have no grammaticised use at all.

contrast.text: The mural was restored by a volunteer. [by marks the passive agent]
The volunteer waited by the gate. [by has spatial meaning; non-grammaticised]
the demolition of the warehouse [of links an NP to the noun demolition]
The athlete was pleased with the result. [with is selected by the adjective pleased]

rules.review_notes: The source states virtually restricted to NP complements in grammaticised uses, not an exceptionless ban on other complements. No free-modifier prohibition is converted into an unsourced global error rule.

rules.statement: Individual prepositions select different complement categories, including NP, PP, AdvP, interrogative clause, and predicative AdjP, so a complement category available after one preposition need not be licensed by another.
rules.condition: When analysing a PP, determine the category and grammatical function licensed by its specific head rather than assuming every preposition accepts the same complement types; for example until licenses an AdvP, on an interrogative clause, and for a predicative AdjP.

contrast.text: The cat emerged from behind the wardrobe. [PP complement of from]
The museum remained closed until quite recently. [AdvP complement of until]
The group disagreed on whether the bridge was safe. [interrogative clause complement of on]
The hikers took the stranger for dead. [predicative AdjP complement of for]

rules.review_notes: The source explicitly contrasts until (AdvP permitted, interrogative clause excluded) with on (interrogative clause permitted, AdvP excluded). Examples demonstrate licensed positive patterns; this classification is not an unrestricted grammar checker prohibition.

rules.statement: A very small set of English prepositions, including notwithstanding, can follow their NP complement inside PP structure instead of preceding it.
rules.condition: For the exceptional preposition notwithstanding, recognise both head-before-complement and complement-before-head structures as PPs; do not confuse complement-before-head order with preposition stranding in a non-canonical clause.

contrast.text: Notwithstanding the storm, the crew continued. [head before NP complement]
The storm notwithstanding, the crew continued. [NP complement before head]
Which storm were they discussing? [ordinary fronting, not a postposed-preposition PP]
